briefs.nephrotic-child:
Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child

protein on a routine dipstick in a well child · nephrotic or nephritic · the lesion, and the age-directed search for its causeIs the protein still there in a first-morning urine, are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?

Routine dipstickWhich lesionMembranousPractice
Bottom line
  • Orthostatic proteinuria: protein in urine made while upright, with a normal first-morning sample after lying down all night; most common in adolescent boys.
  • Transient proteinuria: protein during fever, exercise, stress, cold or dehydration that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes.
  • Persistent proteinuria: a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio above 0.2 mg/mg (above 0.5 at 6 to 24 months), or protein with an abnormal urinalysis; it needs a renal workup.
  • Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia; blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) usually normal, which is what separates it from nephritic disease.
  • Minimal change disease: about 80% of nephrotic syndrome in children, and the default in a young child.
  • Membranous nephropathy: subepithelial immune deposits with granular immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement component 3 (C3) along the capillary loops; usually primary in adults, rare and usually secondary in children.
Protein on a routine dipstick in a well child

A well child with protein on a routine dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria; both are benign, so the first step is to repeat the urinalysis, before any imaging, steroids or biopsy. Protein with blood, hypertension or edema points to glomerular disease from the start: that child goes straight to the renal workup.

Management ladder: incidental proteinuria in a well child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Repeat the urine on a first-morning sample, after any fever or hard exercise has passed: dipstick, microscopy and protein-to-creatinine ratio; a bedtime sample alongside shows the orthostatic patternFirst-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg, or blood, casts, hypertension or edema
StopNormal first-morning sample (ratio 0.2 mg/mg or less, or 0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months, with a normal urinalysis): reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 yearProtein returns on a first-morning sample
2Persistent proteinuria: complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine; add albumin, complement or renal ultrasound as the history and exam directHematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis
3Pediatric nephrology referral; renal biopsy is considered for those featuresTop rung
Protein on a routine dipstick: the differential
DiagnosisThe tellIn a well adolescent
Orthostatic proteinuriaBenign upright leak; protein at bedtime, none on wakingCommon in adolescent boys; the timed repeat confirms it
Transient proteinuriaA trigger; gone on any repeat once wellNo recent trigger; the same repeat sorts it out
Nephrotic syndromeMinimal change disease in a young child; edema, 3+ to 4+ protein, ratio above 2 mg/mg, low albuminNormal examination, no edema
GlomerulonephritisPoststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy, lupus; blood and red cell casts, hypertension, rising creatinineNormal blood pressure; protein is the only urine finding

The child with proteinuria: nephrotic versus nephritic, then which lesion
LesionMechanism and tellAgainst it when the biopsy shows membranous
Minimal change diseaseCytokine podocyte injury; abrupt onset, no hematuria, normal blood pressure; normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, foot process effacement on electron microscopySubacute course and a positive immunofluorescence
Membranous nephropathyImmune complexes, the nephrotic exception; subacute; adult primary, child secondaryThe diagnosis; the question is its cause
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisImmune complexes about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo; nephritic: hematuria, hypertension, raised creatinine, low C3No red cells, normal blood pressure and creatinine

Membranous nephropathy: age directs the search

When the biopsy already names membranous nephropathy, only the search for a cause remains. In adults it is usually primary (autoantibodies to endogenous podocyte antigens) and once infection, autoimmune disease and drugs are excluded the search ends with malignancy screening for age; in children it is rare and usually secondary, so a pediatric case is secondary until proven otherwise, and finding the cause is the management. The highest-yield cause is hepatitis B: circulating immune complexes of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBeAg deposit subepithelially and produce exactly this picture.

Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy has 1 month of facial puffiness and fatigue periorbital and pretibial edema urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells, no casts renal biopsy: subepithelial deposits, granular IgG and C3 BP 110/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.2 g/dL · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Hepatitis B serologies → membranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so the biopsy names the lesion but obliges a search for its cause, and hepatitis B is the highest-yield cause to test. Antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which needs hematuria and hypertension, and strep is not associated with membranous; stopping leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding it is the management
  2. 15-year-old boy at a sports physical afternoon dipstick: 2+ protein; a second afternoon sample a week later shows the same first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.1 mg/mg microscopy normal BP 116/70 mm Hg · examination normal → Orthostatic proteinuria → protein in urine made upright with a normal first-morning ratio (0.2 mg/mg or less) is orthostatic proteinuria: reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 year. Transient protein follows fever, exercise or dehydration and is gone on any repeat; persistent proteinuria needs a first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg or an abnormal urinalysis
  3. 11-year-old boy with 2+ protein and 2+ blood on a routine dipstick microscopy shows red cell casts no edema Well; no recent fever or hard exercise BP 138/90 mm Hg → Referral to pediatric nephrology → protein with blood, casts and hypertension is glomerular disease from the start, not a benign pattern, so it goes straight to the renal workup and pediatric nephrology. A first-morning repeat is for protein alone in a well child, and a prednisone trial treats nephrotic syndrome, while this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet
  4. 4-year-old boy has periorbital swelling that began abruptly urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood renal biopsy: light microscopy normal, immunofluorescence negative electron microscopy: diffuse foot process effacement Afebrile · BP 94/56 mm Hg → Minimal change disease → abrupt onset with normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence and foot process effacement on electron microscopy is minimal change disease; a typical young child is treated with empiric corticosteroids without a biopsy, which is kept for atypical features. Membranous shows subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 and a subacute onset; focal segmental glomerulosclerosis shows segmental sclerosis on light microscopy
  5. 58-year-old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling biopsy: subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis serologies negative antinuclear antibody and thyroid studies normal Takes no medications BP 128/80 mm Hg · albumin 2.4 g/dL → Malignancy screening for his age → with infection, autoimmune disease (lupus, thyroiditis) and drugs excluded, the leading remaining secondary association in an adult is malignancy, mostly solid tumors, so screen as appropriate for his age. A repeat biopsy names the same lesion again but not its cause, and stopping is almost never right while a secondary-cause list remains
  6. 9-year-old girl with acute otitis media has 1+ protein on a dipstick T 39.2 °C 2 weeks later she is afebrile afternoon and first-morning urines both negative for protein Otherwise healthy → Transient proteinuria → protein during a fever that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes is transient proteinuria and needs no further testing. Orthostatic proteinuria keeps protein in the upright afternoon sample, and persistent proteinuria keeps it on the first-morning sample
  7. 4-year-old girl has 5 days of periorbital and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood creatinine and complement levels normal Previously healthy; growth normal Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · albumin 1.9 g/dL → Oral prednisone without a renal biopsy → a typical young child with edema, pure 4+ proteinuria and a normal blood pressure, creatinine and complement has presumed minimal change disease: corticosteroids without a biopsy, and most children remit. Biopsy is for an older child or atypical features, and furosemide alone with a repeat urinalysis delays the corticosteroids that bring the remission
  8. 8-year-old boy has cola-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago No prior episodes of dark urine urinalysis: blood and red cell casts BP 140/90 mm Hg · creatinine 1.6 mg/dL · C3 low → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → a nephritic picture about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis (up to about 6 weeks after impetigo), with hematuria, hypertension, a raised creatinine and a low C3, is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: supportive care and blood pressure control. Membranous is nephrotic, with protein and usually no red cells or casts; IgA nephropathy brings hematuria during or within days of a respiratory infection, not 2 weeks later
  9. 16-year-old boy with chronic hepatitis B has 1 month of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells biopsy: granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits BP 112/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.0 g/dL → Deposited hepatitis B e antigen immune complexes → circulating immune complexes of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBeAg deposit in the subepithelial space and give the granular IgG and C3 along the loops. That granular IgG is antibody in the deposits, so neither direct viral injury to the podocytes nor complement activation alone accounts for the picture
  10. 16-year-old boy with 1+ protein on a dipstick at a sports physical no blood in the urine No fever, illness or hard exercise this week Examination normal BP 114/70 mm Hg → First-morning urine protein-to-creatinine ratio → a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2 mg/mg or less on waking fits orthostatic or transient proteinuria. An afternoon sample is made upright, so it shows the orthostatic leak rather than excluding it, and the spot ratio replaces the 24-hour collection, which is impractical in children
  11. 5-year-old boy, 1 week of swelling and fatigue Body mass index 98th percentile; daily multivitamin periorbital, pretibial edema scrotum mildly swollen, nontender; abdomen normal urine: 4+ protein, no blood or casts BP 92/55 mm Hg · HR 90/min · specific gravity 1.028 → Cytokine-induced glomerular injury → pure proteinuria with no blood, a normal blood pressure and dependent edema at age 5 is minimal change disease: T-cell cytokines such as interleukin 13 injure the podocytes. Obesity is a real focal segmental glomerulosclerosis association, but that lesion is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; immune complex deposition (poststreptococcal, membranoproliferative) brings hematuria, and membranous, the immune complex exception without hematuria, is rare at age 5
  12. 13-year-old boy with 2+ protein on a dipstick at a well visit first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.6 mg/mg on two separate days microscopy: no blood or casts BP 108/66 mm Hg · no edema → Complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine → a first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg is persistent proteinuria, which needs a basic renal workup; albumin, complement or a renal ultrasound are added as the history and examination direct. Reassurance is only for a normal first-morning sample, and biopsy is considered after hematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis appear
  13. 12-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria on repeated urinalyses Two maternal uncles have kidney failure No sore throat or recent illness; growth normal No edema; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · BP 108/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL → Audiology evaluation → persistent hematuria with kidney failure in maternal uncles points to Alport syndrome, an X-linked type IV collagen defect whose partner finding is sensorineural hearing loss, so test hearing. Hepatitis B serologies search for the cause of membranous nephropathy, which is nephrotic; antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows strep pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks (impetigo by up to about 6) with hypertension and a raised creatinine
  14. 17-year-old girl has 5 weeks of facial and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells or casts biopsy: granular IgG and C3, subepithelial deposits No serologies sent yet BP 108/68 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Stopping the workup at the biopsy → membranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so stopping at the biopsy leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding the cause is the management. Hepatitis B and C serologies and an antinuclear antibody (for systemic lupus erythematosus) are the secondary-cause search and should go ahead
  15. 66-year-old man has 3 months of leg swelling and exertional dyspnea urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells echocardiography: restrictive cardiomyopathy renal biopsy: apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain BP 118/72 mm Hg · albumin 2.1 g/dL → Amyloidosis → nephrotic-range protein in an older adult with apple-green birefringence and a restrictive cardiomyopathy is amyloidosis, and echocardiography shows the cardiac involvement. The biopsy shows amyloid, not the immune deposits with granular IgG and C3 of membranous nephropathy or the normal light microscopy of minimal change disease
  16. 14-year-old boy with 3+ protein on a dipstick at a routine visit no edema no blood in the urine No repeat sample collected yet; feels well BP 110/68 mm Hg → Trial of oral prednisone → steroids treat nephrotic syndrome, not an unconfirmed dipstick finding; this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet. A first-morning repeat and urine microscopy for red cells and casts are the right first steps
  17. 15-year-old boy with severe obesity has 2 months of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein and microscopic hematuria no remission after a full course of prednisone Afebrile · BP 138/90 mm Hg → Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis → obesity with hematuria, hypertension and steroid resistance points to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (segmental sclerosis on light microscopy), and these atypical features earn a renal biopsy. Minimal change disease brings no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a steroid response; membranous is subacute, usually secondary in a child, and its blood pressure is typically normal
How NBME framed it: question 1

12-year-old boy at a well-child visit No illnesses since his visit a year ago HR 102/min · respiratory rate 21/min · BP 102/60 mm Hg examination normal urinalysis: 3+ protein

Most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Intravenous pyelography: images the collecting system for anatomic lesions and strictures; but it cannot show whether the protein persists.
  • Trial of corticosteroids: treats nephrotic syndrome; but this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet, and transient or orthostatic proteinuria is benign.
  • Renal biopsy: diagnoses persistent glomerular disease; but it is invasive and comes only after persistence or red-flag features are shown.

Down to two: repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking, or renal ultrasonography. Repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking: a well boy with protein on one dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria, and orthostatic proteinuria, common in adolescent boys, shows protein at bedtime and a normal first-morning sample. Ultrasonography looks for obstruction, abscess, cysts or masses and cannot show whether the protein persists; it is at most a later, selective test. The key named the timed procedure, not orthostatic proteinuria.

Membranous nephropathy Hepatitis B – evaluating every patient with membranous nephropathy for it is recommended; in a child it is close to mandatory · Secondary causes – infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis), malignancy (solid tumors in adults), autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroiditis), drugs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, penicillamine) · Tempo – gradual podocyte damage gives a subacute onset over weeks to a month; deposits accumulate slowly, while foot processes efface suddenly in minimal change disease · Course – blood pressure and GFR typically normal; partial or complete remission common, end-stage disease rare
Minimal change disease Mechanism – T-cell dysregulation releases cytokines such as interleukin 13 that injure podocytes; the capillary wall loses its charge selectivity, anionic albumin leaks, and low oncotic pressure gives dependent edema (periorbital, scrotal, pretibial) · Diagnosis – clinical; biopsy only for atypical features · Treatment – corticosteroids without a biopsy; most children remit, relapse is common, and the risk of chronic kidney disease is low when steroid responsive · Obesity – a real FSGS association, but FSGS is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a pure 4+ protein urinalysis mean minimal change disease
Read the urine Nephrotic versus nephritic is settled on the urinalysis, not the protein: 4+ protein with hypoalbuminemia and edema, without red cells or casts and with a normal blood pressure and creatinine, is nephrotic; red cells, hypertension and a rising creatinine are nephritic. Deposits: subepithelial is membranous, subendothelial is lupus nephritis, mesangial is IgA nephropathy. Up to 10% of school-age children show protein on a single screen; with repeated testing, about 0.1% do. Orthostatic proteinuria affects about 2% to 5% of adolescents, more often boys, and long-term follow-up shows no progressive kidney disease. A first-morning spot ratio replaces the 24-hour collection, which is impractical in children. A dipstick can read falsely positive in very concentrated urine (specific gravity above 1.030) or alkaline urine (pH above 8).
Common wrong answers After a membranous biopsy in a teenager: no additional workup: the biopsy names the lesion but not the cause, and stopping is almost never right when a secondary-cause list exists. Antistreptolysin O: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is nephritic, with hematuria, hypertension and a raised creatinine. Audiology: deafness belongs to Alport syndrome, which presents with hematuria, not nephrotic-range protein. Echocardiography: amyloidosis pairs nephrotic syndrome with cardiac disease, but a membranous biopsy shows immune deposits, and a teenager is the wrong age. Renal biopsy for a well child's dipstick: invasive, and only after persistence or red-flag features. Corticosteroid trial: treats nephrotic syndrome, and the well child has no edema and no diagnosis. Renal ultrasonography and intravenous pyelography: they look for obstruction, abscess, cysts, masses, anatomic lesions or strictures, and cannot show whether the protein persists.
Pairs with Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome: the nephritic side of this fork, the Alport link, the parallel well child with isolated microscopic hematuria, and red cells, hypertension, a rising creatinine and a low C3 weeks after strep. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes: from the chief complaint to this diagnosis, with relapse, peritonitis, thrombosis and vaccines in the nephrotic child.
Transferable rule

In a well child with protein on a routine dipstick, repeat the urine on a first-morning sample before any imaging, steroids or biopsy; only protein that persists on waking, or protein with blood, hypertension or edema, needs a renal workup. When a biopsy diagnosis is given, decide what it obliges you to do next: ask what the disease is associated with, and let the patient's age decide whether that list is the priority or an afterthought.
